# Global minimum counts for separable CPWL functions in every dimension

Both archived manuscripts solve the one-dimensional slope-jump problem, including common-bend cancellation. This report adds arbitrary-dimensional separable inputs, and its lower bound is over every convex CPWL decomposition, including nonseparable ones on unrelated complexes.

Let
\[
f(x)=a\cdot x+b+\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}\delta_{ij}(x_i-t_{ij})_+,
\]
where for each$i$ the$t_{ij}$ are distinct sorted real numbers and$\delta_{ij}\ne0$. Put$p_i=\#\{j:\delta_{ij}>0\}$ and$q_i=\#\{j:\delta_{ij}<0\}$. Count the maximal full-dimensional affine regions of each convex function, with an affine function having one piece. The simultaneous coordinatewise minima are exactly
\[
\min\#G=\prod_i(p_i+1),\qquad
\min\#H=\prod_i(q_i+1),\qquad f=G-H.
\]
In particular the same decomposition minimizes the sum, maximum, and every coordinatewise increasing objective of these two counts.

For the construction put the affine term and all positive hinges in$g$, and all negative hinges, with positive coefficients, in$h$. Both are convex and$g-h=f$. The positive coordinate hyperplanes split space into$\prod_i(p_i+1)$ open boxes, allowing unbounded intervals. On each box$g$ is affine. Crossing a positive hinge changes its$i$th gradient component by a strictly positive amount. Two distinct boxes therefore have distinct gradients: select a coordinate whose interval differs, and that coordinate's accumulated positive jump differs. These boxes are exactly the maximal full-dimensional affine regions. The identical argument with negative hinges counts$h$.

The point needing an unrestricted proof is that extra, possibly oblique, bends in another pair cannot reduce those products. Let$f=G-H$ be any convex CPWL pair. Consider one positive hinge hyperplane$x_i=t$ and a relatively open point$z$ on it away from all other hinge hyperplanes of$f$. On a sufficiently short line through$z$ parallel to$e_i$, the slope jump of$f$ is the corresponding$\delta>0$. Convexity makes the jump of$H$ nonnegative. Hence the jump of$G$ is at least$\delta$: $G$ cannot be affine in any neighborhood of$z$.

Every full-dimensional affine region of a convex CPWL function is convex. For example write it as the maximum of its finitely many supporting affine formulas; the domain where a given formula attains this maximum is an intersection of half-spaces. If the interior of such a region met both sides of$x_i=t$, its intersection with that hyperplane would contain a relatively open subset. This subset contains a$z$ avoiding the other finitely many hinge hyperplanes, contradicting the forced positive bend just proved. Thus no full-dimensional affine region of$G$ can meet two positive-grid boxes. Each box is open and nonempty, and is covered by finitely many closed affine domains, so it contains the interior of at least one of them. There must therefore be at least one distinct region for each box. This proves the lower bound for$G$. Applying the same argument to$-f=H-G$ proves the lower bound for$H$.

The argument also treats zero counts and affine inputs, using empty products of break hyperplanes and one interval per coordinate. It needs distinct break positions per coordinate after merging coincident hinges and discarding zero jumps. It does not assume generic position between the two unknown decompositions, nor count only a chosen grid subdivision.

For rational hinge input the formulas give a finite exact construction. Sorting and merging costs$O(\sum_i m_i\log(m_i+1))$ rational comparisons; sign splitting and prefix sums are polynomial in the full binary input length. The hinge representation has linear input-size length, while an explicit enumeration of all affine formulas can have the displayed product-size output and must pay for that output. No polynomial bound in a compact representation is falsely asserted for enumerating exponentially many pieces.

The primary decomposition-polyhedra paper distinguishes unrestricted global minimality from minimality compatible with a fixed complex. Its general fixed-complex theorem alone would not prove the unrestricted lower bound above. The result here supplies a separable infinite family in every dimension; interactions among oblique hinge hyperplanes and general CPWL functions remain open in this report.
